en: 2,500 people stand on a grid with three types: Orderly (wait quietly), Cutter, and Punisher (waits in line, but punishes cutters when they see one).

Each round every person meets their 8 neighbors once and collects points. A cutter gains when meeting an Orderly person, who loses the same amount. When a cutter meets a Punisher, the gain is reduced by the punishment's effect, and Punishers pay a cost for punishing.
Everyone copies the type of the highest-scoring person among their neighbors. With a tiny probability, a new person arrives as Orderly or Cutter.
Gain from cutting <output id="o-gain"></output>
Time saved by one cut
Punishment effect <output id="o-punish"></output>
How much a cutter's gain shrinks when punished
Punishment cost <output id="o-cost"></output>
The cost paid by the one who punishes
Initial share of cutters <output id="o-cutters"></output>
People who cut at the start
Initial share of punishers <output id="o-punishers"></output>
People who punished at the start
① How the Line Changes
Each cell is one person. Blue is Orderly, red is Cutter, green is Punisher. Watch which color spreads from where.
② Share of Each Type Over Time
The stacked area is the whole (100%). Cutters grow at first, but see what happens next.
Orderly
Cutter

③ As Punishment Gets Stronger
The horizontal axis is the punishment effect, the vertical axis is the share of cutters left after 100 rounds. Dots are 5 runs.
④ How Many Punishers Do We Need at the Start?
The horizontal axis is the initial share of punishers, the vertical axis is the share of cutters after 100 rounds.

What it shows: Cutting spreads fast at first because it pays, but if enough people punish cutters and the punishment outweighs the gain, cutting dies out again. Conversely, if there are too few punishers or punishing is too costly, order collapses. Order isn't kept by itself; someone pays a price to keep it.

What it doesn't show: It doesn't mean real queues are this simple. In reality, cutting is also deterred by laws, staff intervention and social reputation, none of which are in this model. The assumption that no new punishers appear also differs from reality. The gains and costs are relative numbers for comparison.

A grid model in the style of spatial evolutionary games (Nowak, May (1992), "Evolutionary games and spatial chaos", Nature 359): play with neighbors and copy the strategy of the best-scoring neighbor. Adding the "punishing cooperator" is this project's own design, not a reproduction of the paper's numbers.

If the gain is smaller than the cost (e.g., gain 0.1, cost 0.2), punishing is a net loss, so Punishers vanish first and cutting spreads. At the extreme gain of 1.0 Orderly people lose heavily and results can change, so the slider is capped at 1.0.
Graphs ③ and ④ change only the given value in the same setup and run 5 times each for 100 rounds. You can verify with node tools/validate-more.js queue.

How Does a Revolution Begin? · Simulatio Lab
When does a few people stepping forward turn into thousands? Run the threshold model yourself and see how collective action tips.

Sometimes hundreds gather and nothing happens; sometimes a handful of sparks fill the whole square. Why do outcomes split so sharply among the same kind of people? With one simple rule, "decide whether to join by seeing how many others have come out," we look at when collective action spreads.

Each of the 1,000 people has a "threshold": they join once at least this share of everyone is already in the square. Low-threshold people join easily; high-threshold people join only after a crowd has formed.
Thresholds follow a normal distribution (0–100%) with a mean and a spread. A few people are instigators with a threshold of 0, who step forward even when nobody is there.
Each round, everyone whose threshold is at or below "the share already out" steps forward. It ends when no one new joins.
Dots are people, colored from yellow (early) to red (late) by the round they joined. A black ring marks an instigator.
Mean threshold <output id="o-mean"></output>
Larger means a harder place to step forward
Threshold spread <output id="o-spread"></output>
Larger means thresholds vary more
Share of instigators <output id="o-radicals"></output>
People who step forward first (threshold 0)
Threshold distribution <output id="o-mode"></output>

① The Square
Each dot is a person, with low-threshold people at the top left and high-threshold people at the bottom right. Watch how the crowd spreads round by round.
② Where Does It Stop?

The blue curve is "the share who will join next if this many are already out." While the curve is above the diagonal (y=x) the crowd keeps growing, and it stops where the curve meets the diagonal. The red staircase is the actual path.
③ Participation Over Time
Shows how the share of people in the square changes over rounds. See whether it grows slowly at first and then bursts.
④ When the Mean Threshold Changes
The horizontal axis is the mean threshold, the vertical axis is the share in the square at the end. Dots are 6 runs, and the gray line is the case with no instigators at all.

What it shows: Among the very same people, the outcome can split between "the square fills up" and "nothing happens," depending on whether there is a spark and how varied the thresholds are. With the same mean threshold, more varied thresholds let the cascade continue more easily, and with no spark at all nothing starts however low the mean is. In the classic example, changing just one person with a 1% threshold turns a square where all 100 join into one that stops at 1.

What it doesn't show: It does not mean real revolutions or protests unfold by these numbers, and it takes no side and predicts nothing. Reality has information, fear, organization, government responses and social networks; this model is a very simple society where people decide only by "the share of others who have come out." People's thresholds are invisible in reality, and the numbers here are settings chosen for explanation.
